Frames the concern constructively as a clarifying question
Describes doing appropriate homework before raising it
Appropriately holds the position if genuine concern remains after pushback

questions.title: Deciding When to Stop an Experiment That Isn't Working
questions.prompt: You've personally invested three weeks into an experiment direction that keeps almost-but-not-quite working, and you keep believing one more tweak will fix it. How do you decide whether to keep going or cut your losses, and how do you communicate that decision?
questions.modelAnswer:
A strong answer recognizes the sunk-cost trap directly -- the three weeks already invested are not a valid input to the decision about whether to continue, since that time is spent regardless of what happens next, and the only question that should matter is whether the expected value of continuing (probability the next tweak actually works, times the value of it working, versus the compute and time cost of finding out) looks better than the expected value of stopping and redirecting that time elsewhere -- 'I've already put in three weeks' is exactly the reasoning pattern that keeps people chasing a failing direction well past the point a fresh, unbiased assessment would recommend stopping.

A concrete practice for making this assessment honestly rather than through self-serving optimism is keeping an explicit log of each tweak tried, what was predicted to happen, and what actually happened -- if the pattern across several tweaks shows genuine, if slow, directional progress (each fix gets closer, even if not there yet), continuing a bit longer with a specific, pre-committed stopping point is reasonable; if the pattern shows no clear trend, or each 'almost-fix' turns out to reveal a new, different problem rather than closing in on the original one, that's a strong signal the 'almost there' feeling is an illusion rather than genuine progress, and the honest read of the log should override the gut feeling.

Communicating the decision to stop (if that's the conclusion) should be straightforward and unemotional about what was learned and why continuing doesn't look like the right bet going forward, not framed as personal failure -- and proactively asking a colleague or manager for a second opinion on the log/evidence before finalizing the decision is a good practice specifically because someone who hasn't spent three weeks personally invested is less susceptible to the same sunk-cost-driven optimism and can give a more objective read on whether 'one more tweak' is a reasonable bet or wishful thinking.
questions.professionalAnswer:
The three weeks I've already put in aren't actually a valid input to this decision -- that time's spent either way, and 'I've already invested three weeks' is exactly the reasoning pattern that keeps people chasing a failing direction well past where a fresh, unbiased look would say to stop. The only question that should matter is whether continuing looks better in expectation than redirecting that time elsewhere -- what's the real probability the next tweak works, what's it worth if it does, against the cost of finding out.

What I'd actually do to check this honestly, instead of trusting my own optimism, is keep an explicit log of every tweak I've tried, what I predicted would happen, and what actually happened. If that log shows genuine, if slow, directional progress -- each attempt gets a bit closer, even if it's not there yet -- continuing a bit longer with a specific, pre-committed stopping point is reasonable. If the log shows no clear trend, or each 'almost there' fix just reveals a new, different problem instead of closing in on the original one, that's a strong signal the 'almost there' feeling is an illusion, not real progress -- and I'd trust the log over the gut feeling.

If the honest read says stop, I'd communicate that straightforwardly -- what we learned, why continuing doesn't look like a good bet going forward -- not framed as a personal failure. And before I finalize that call, I'd actually go ask a colleague or my manager for a second opinion on the log and the evidence, specifically because someone who hasn't spent three weeks personally invested is a lot less susceptible to the same sunk-cost optimism I'm fighting, and can give me a more objective read on whether 'one more tweak' is a real bet or just wishful thinking.
commonMistakes: Treating the already-invested three weeks as a valid reason to continue (the sunk-cost fallacy)
Relying on gut feeling ('I think this one will work') rather than an honest log of predicted vs. actual outcomes
Not setting a pre-committed stopping point even when continuing a bit longer is the reasonable call
Framing a decision to stop as personal failure rather than a straightforward, unemotional communication
Not seeking an outside, less-invested perspective before finalizing the decision
keyPoints: Already-invested time is a sunk cost and should not factor into the continue/stop decision
An explicit log of tweaks, predictions, and actual outcomes gives an honest signal over gut feeling
Genuine directional progress in the log supports continuing with a pre-committed stopping point
A flat or confound-revealing pattern in the log signals the 'almost there' feeling is likely an illusion
Seeking a less-invested colleague's second opinion counters one's own sunk-cost-driven optimism

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies and rejects the sunk-cost reasoning trap
Proposes a concrete, honest method for assessing actual progress
Gives a clear, well-reasoned continue/stop decision criterion
Proposes seeking an outside perspective before finalizing

questions.title: Being Asked to Cut Corners on Safety Evaluation Under Deadline Pressure
questions.prompt: A product launch is scheduled for next week, and a manager asks whether the safety evaluation suite can be shortened to meet the deadline, since 'the full suite has never actually found anything on a model this similar to the last one.' How do you respond?
questions.modelAnswer:
A strong answer treats this request seriously and respectfully rather than reacting defensively, while being clear and firm that the evaluation suite's purpose is specifically to catch the case where something is different this time -- 'it's never found anything before' is true of every safety check that hasn't yet caught a real issue, right up until the one time it does, and that specific framing of the request should be named explicitly as the reasoning pattern it is, since agreeing to shorten evaluation specifically because it hasn't found problems before undermines the entire premise of running it in the first place.

The candidate should engage constructively with the actual constraint rather than just saying a flat no: asking what specifically is driving the deadline pressure, and whether there's a way to meet it that doesn't involve cutting the safety evaluation itself -- is the deadline genuinely fixed, or is it more flexible than initially presented once the alternative is 'launch with reduced safety evaluation' spelled out explicitly; is there a way to parallelize or accelerate the evaluation itself (more compute thrown at running the suite faster, rather than running less of it) that solves the actual time problem without reducing coverage. A collaborative problem-solving posture that takes the deadline constraint seriously, while being unmovable on not reducing safety evaluation coverage to meet it, is more productive than either an inflexible refusal to engage or a quiet concession.

If the deadline genuinely cannot be met without reducing evaluation scope, the candidate should make the tradeoff and its risk explicit to whoever has the authority to accept that risk, rather than making the call themselves informally or quietly complying -- this is exactly the kind of decision that should go through whatever formal process exists for this (a responsible scaling policy's evaluation gate, or equivalent), and a direct statement that this decision needs to be made explicitly by someone with the authority and accountability to own that risk, not resolved informally between the candidate and one manager under deadline pressure, is the core of a strong answer here.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I'd take this seriously and respond respectfully, not defensively, but I'd be clear and firm: the whole reason this suite exists is to catch the case where something's different this time. 'It's never found anything before' is true of literally every safety check right up until the one time it actually does find something, and I'd name that reasoning pattern explicitly, because agreeing to shorten evaluation specifically on the grounds that it hasn't found problems before undermines the entire premise of running it at all.

I wouldn't just say a flat no, though -- I'd engage with the actual constraint. What's driving the deadline, and is there a way to meet it without cutting the evaluation itself? Is the deadline genuinely fixed, or does it get more flexible once 'launch with reduced safety evaluation' is spelled out explicitly as the alternative? Is there a way to throw more resources at running the full suite faster, rather than running less of it, that actually solves the time problem without cutting coverage? I'd rather be a collaborative problem-solver on the deadline while being completely unmovable on not reducing safety evaluation coverage to hit it.

If it genuinely turns out the deadline can't be met without cutting scope, I wouldn't make that call myself informally, and I wouldn't quietly go along with it either. I'd make the tradeoff and its actual risk explicit to whoever has the authority to accept that risk -- this is exactly the kind of decision that should go through whatever formal process exists for it, a responsible scaling policy's evaluation gate or equivalent. This needs to be decided explicitly by someone with the authority and accountability to own that risk, not resolved informally between me and one manager under deadline pressure.

questions.title: Onboarding and Mentoring a New Research Engineer Joining the Team
questions.prompt: A new research engineer is joining your team, strong in general software engineering but with limited prior ML research experience. How do you approach onboarding and mentoring them over their first month?
questions.modelAnswer:
A strong answer tailors onboarding to the specific gap (research-specific intuitions and practices, not general software engineering ability) rather than a generic onboarding checklist -- the candidate should describe starting with small, well-scoped tasks that build research-specific judgment (reproducing a known, already-understood result from the team's prior work, which teaches the team's codebase and conventions while having a known-correct answer to check against) rather than throwing the new engineer directly at open-ended research ambiguity, since general software engineering skill doesn't automatically transfer to judgment calls like 'is this result real or an artifact' or 'what's a reasonable ablation to run here,' which take time and exposure to develop.

Pairing the new engineer with an experienced team member for their first few real experiments, specifically on tasks like interpreting ambiguous results or deciding what to try next when something doesn't work as expected, builds the research-specific judgment that's the actual gap, while the new engineer's strong software engineering skill should be explicitly leveraged early and visibly (perhaps contributing to or improving the shared research codebase/infrastructure, where their existing strength is directly valuable) so the onboarding period builds confidence and visible contribution rather than feeling like a long period of only being taught with nothing to contribute.

The candidate should also set explicit, realistic expectations about the onboarding timeline with the new engineer directly -- being honest that developing research-specific judgment (distinguishing a real finding from noise, knowing when a result is surprising enough to investigate further versus expected enough to move on) takes real time and exposure, not just reading documentation, so the new engineer doesn't feel like they should already have this judgment by week two and doesn't become discouraged by a mismatch between their strong general engineering competence and their appropriately-still-developing research-specific judgment -- normalizing that this gap is expected and closes with experience, not something to be anxious about.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I'd tailor this to the specific gap -- research-specific intuitions and practices, not general engineering ability, which they already clearly have. I'd start them with small, well-scoped tasks that build research judgment specifically -- reproducing a known, already-understood result from the team's prior work is a good first one, because it teaches the codebase and conventions while having a known-correct answer to check their work against, rather than throwing them straight into open-ended research ambiguity where they don't yet have the judgment to know if something's gone wrong.

I'd pair them with an experienced team member for their first few real experiments, specifically on the parts that are actually hard to develop -- interpreting an ambiguous result, deciding what to try next when something doesn't work the way you expected. That's the real gap, and it takes exposure, not documentation, to build. At the same time, I'd lean into their existing strength early and visibly -- have them contribute to or improve the shared research codebase or infrastructure, somewhere their software engineering skill is directly and obviously valuable, so onboarding isn't just a month of being taught with nothing to show for it.

I'd also be upfront with them directly about the timeline -- developing research-specific judgment, telling a real finding apart from noise, knowing when a result is surprising enough to dig into versus expected enough to move past, genuinely takes time and exposure, not just reading. I wouldn't want them feeling like they should already have that judgment by week two just because their general engineering is strong -- I'd normalize that this gap is completely expected and closes with experience, not something to be anxious about.

questions.title: Balancing Exploratory Research Freedom Against Deliverable Deadlines
questions.prompt: Your manager wants a specific deliverable (a working demo) in three weeks, but your instinct as a researcher is that a more exploratory, less certain approach would produce a better long-term result even though it might not be ready in time. How do you handle this tension?
questions.modelAnswer:
A strong answer treats this as a decision to make transparently with the manager rather than either unilaterally pursuing the exploratory path and hoping it works out, or unilaterally abandoning it to play safe without raising the tension at all -- the candidate should describe explicitly laying out both options for the manager with their real tradeoffs: the safe path reliably delivers something working in three weeks but is more likely to hit a lower ceiling, while the exploratory path has a real chance of a meaningfully better result but carries genuine risk of not being ready at all by the deadline, and the manager (who has visibility into broader deadline pressures and stakeholder expectations the candidate may not have) should be the one making the final call on which risk profile is acceptable, not the researcher making a unilateral bet with the team's deadline.

A concrete practical structure the candidate should propose is a hybrid: pursue the safe path as the committed deliverable that will definitely be ready, while spending a bounded, explicitly time-boxed portion of the three weeks on the exploratory approach as a parallel, lower-commitment track -- this gives the manager certainty about what will actually ship while preserving some chance at the better outcome without betting the entire deliverable on it, and the specific time-box (e.g. the first week, or a fixed number of hours per week) should be agreed with the manager upfront rather than informally squeezed in without visibility.

The candidate should also propose a concrete decision point partway through the three weeks -- a checkpoint where progress on the exploratory track is honestly assessed and a go/no-go call is made about whether to lean further into it or fully commit remaining time to the safe path -- rather than only deciding at the very end when there's no time left to react if the exploratory approach isn't panning out, since an honest mid-point checkpoint preserves the ability to course-correct while there's still time to do so.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I'd treat this as something to lay out transparently with my manager, not something to unilaterally decide either way -- pursuing the exploratory path quietly and hoping it works out, or just abandoning it and playing it safe without even raising the tension. I'd lay out both options honestly: the safe path reliably ships something working in three weeks but probably hits a lower ceiling; the exploratory path has a real shot at something meaningfully better but genuine risk of not being ready at all. My manager has visibility into deadline pressures and stakeholder expectations I might not have, so they should be the one making the final call on what risk profile is actually acceptable here, not me making a unilateral bet with the team's deadline.

What I'd actually propose is a hybrid -- commit to the safe path as the thing that will definitely ship, and spend a bounded, explicitly time-boxed chunk of the three weeks, say the first week, or a fixed number of hours per week, on the exploratory approach as a lower-commitment parallel track. That gives my manager certainty about what's actually going to be ready while preserving a real shot at the better outcome, without betting the whole deliverable on it. And I'd agree that time-box with them upfront, not informally squeeze it in without them knowing.

I'd also want a concrete checkpoint partway through, not just a decision at the very end when there's no time left to react. An honest mid-point check on how the exploratory track is actually going, with a real go/no-go call about whether to lean further in or commit everything that's left to the safe path -- that way if the exploratory approach isn't panning out, there's still time to course-correct instead of finding out on the deadline itself.

questions.title: Responding to a Public Dispute Over Your Model's Benchmark Claims
questions.prompt: A third party publishes a post disputing one of your team's published benchmark results, claiming the number is inflated due to contamination or an unfair comparison. Your initial internal check suggests they might have a partial point. How do you handle the response, internally and externally?

A strong answer prioritizes getting to an accurate internal understanding of what actually happened before any external response, rather than reacting defensively to protect the original claim or capitulating immediately without verification -- the candidate should describe running the specific checks the third party's claim would predict (checking for the contamination pattern they describe, re-running the comparison under the specific conditions they claim were unfair) rather than either dismissing the critique without checking it or assuming it's entirely correct without verification, since the actual goal is determining what's true, not defending a prior claim or capitulating to external pressure.

If the internal check confirms the critique has a valid partial point (which the prompt states is the case here), the candidate should describe acknowledging that specific, confirmed portion clearly and directly rather than issuing a vague, defensive non-response or over-correcting into agreeing with parts of the critique that aren't actually confirmed -- a credible correction states precisely what was found to be accurate in the critique, what the corrected number or methodology actually shows, and what (if anything) in the critique was not confirmed or overstated, since a response that's honest about the confirmed issue while being precise about its actual scope is more credible long-term than either stonewalling or an over-broad mea culpa that concedes more than the evidence supports.

The response should also address the forward-looking process question, not just this specific incident: what changed in the team's evaluation practices to catch this kind of issue earlier next time (the contamination-checking or fair-comparison practices discussed elsewhere), since a credible public response to a legitimate critique includes a concrete statement of what's being done differently going forward, not just an acknowledgment of the specific past error -- this demonstrates the team is treating the critique as useful information that improves future practice, which matters more for long-term credibility than how any single incident is spun.

My first priority is getting to an accurate internal understanding of what actually happened, before any external response goes out at all -- not reacting defensively to protect the original number, and not capitulating immediately either. I'd run the specific checks their claim would predict -- actually check for the contamination pattern they're describing, re-run the comparison under the exact conditions they say were unfair -- rather than either dismissing it unchecked or assuming they're entirely right without verifying it myself. The goal here is figuring out what's true, not defending a prior claim or caving to external pressure.

Given the internal check here confirms they have a partial point, I'd acknowledge that specific, confirmed piece clearly and directly -- not a vague, defensive non-response, and not over-correcting into agreeing with parts of their critique that we didn't actually confirm. A credible correction states exactly what we found to be accurate, what the corrected number or methodology actually shows, and what in their critique wasn't confirmed or was overstated. Being honest about the confirmed issue while staying precise about its actual scope is more credible long-term than either stonewalling or an overly broad apology that concedes more than the evidence actually supports.

And I'd make sure the response addresses the forward-looking piece, not just this one incident -- what are we actually changing in our evaluation practices to catch this kind of issue earlier next time. A credible public response to a legitimate critique includes a concrete statement of what's different going forward, not just an acknowledgment of the one past error. That's what actually matters for long-term credibility -- showing we treat this as useful information that improves how we evaluate going forward, not just managing the optics of one incident.
